topComments.author: spwa4
topComments.text: This is very, very suboptimal. I like the VXLAN support a lot, and of course this will have a lot of features while requiring minimal actual network knowledge (good luck getting everything to work correctly when combined, but you can certainly configure them ... and so you're making it the customer's problem) Oh and this is going to cause out-of-order delivery and slow down user applications by a lot (because of channel bonding that looks like it's just left at the defaults), it is horribly inefficient. People don't put the host network either next to the VMs or on a separate network card for nothing. In their case a packet walk would show: 1) guest userspace -> guest kernel 2) guest kernel virtio_net (hopefully) -> host kernel virtio_net 3) host kernel virtio_net -> host kernel 4) host kernel -> OVS vswitch data path 5) OVS vswitch data path -> host kernel bridge port 6) host kernel bridge port -> host kernel switch/networking stack 7) host kernel switch/networking stack -> host outgoing bonding virtual port 8) host outgoing bonding virtual port -> physical port Each of these steps requires at the very least a memory allocation, inserting a step on a work queue, waiting on that work queue. Also very likely 5 of these steps require a context switch (at minimum waiting for the process scheduler to reschedule a task, on linux still usually requires 1ms minimum wait, more under load). So this inserts 5ms of latency minimum (and under load it's going to balloon) before the packet even arrives on the ring buffer of the first physical network card. And, as stated before, it's also going to cause out-of-order delivery. And that's, of course, before application developers put a multiplication factor before this cost by using something like nginx or even multiple layers of nginx. I get the flexibility gain, and of course application developers get to do whatever they want, but ... why? This is also eating a lot of processing power of the machines (and everything that comes with that, power use, even co2). And a further issue with that is that this is kernel networking path, which doesn't show in top, and doesn't show in most kernel metrics, you have to really know what you're looking for. And the cost that is incurred on the application side by due to the delay and the out of order packets doesn't show up anywhere except on the customer's bill, but good luck finding that it's wasted capacity. If you do something like ML training from an NFS or S3 mount or NVMEoE or RoCE you will clearly notice the flaws in this design. The gains you can make there approach the gains you can make by switching from ethernet to fibre channel/infiniband. What is possible with a great design: 0/1 context switch from guest userspace to network card ring buffer (zero context switches is possible by either using io/uring in guest userspace, or by binding the physical hardware to the guest VM and then into the application). Ping times to same-building VMs that consistently stay below 0.1ms, even with machine loads over 98%. Wish someone would pay me to do that. Zero context switches while maintaining all features is possible. A lot of work, but possible. I don't believe anyone has yet done it, but it is possible. And, please, move the linux host into the OVS ... just that little step will save about half the cost and it only requires being a bit more careful in operations (or having actual OOB, like serial or an extra hardware network card, the cheapest thing you're throwing away will easily do for that purpose) And yes, I worked on the networking stack of one of the hyperscalers. They are at 2 to 3 context switches, more if you use any kind of tunneling (it's a crime that VXLAN is not supported ...). A lot better than this design, but not really close to perfectly optimal. It would be great to work on getting that closer to optimal in a large hoster. VPP + DPDK right into guest VMs. Sigh. Back to AI networking.

topComments.author: schopra909
topComments.text: Hi HN, author here! For context, we're a 2-person lab training generative video models. Goal is a new set of controllable, animation tools (you can read more about that here https://www.linum.ai/about if you're curious). The biggest bottleneck for our last text-to-video model in terms of training and inference cost is attention. Video models are incredibly token dense (e.g. 110K tokens for a several second clip). If we can condense that context window more aggressively, we can train bigger models for a lot less $$ and offer them to prosumers at reasonable price points (unlike the big models today like Seedance, which cost an arm and a leg to run). Traditionally, image and video models have two disjoint components: VAE (Variational Autoencoder) and Diffusion Transformer (DiT). They're trained separately, and empirically VAEs seems to struggle to get past 16x16 token reduction. Here, we're switching to pixel-space, throwing away the VAE, and achieving 32x32 token reduction (4x smaller context windows) while learning a better overall model in a fraction of the training samples. The central thesis is "simpler is better". If we can put the compression problem into the more powerful Diffusion Transformer (DiT) would should be able to learn a "latent space" optimized for generation and get better compression without hurting generation quality. stackOverflowQuestions.title: Is PostgreSQL data recoverable after an accidental TRUNCATE CASCADE when the schema and tables still exist but are empty?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: Suppose a PostgreSQL 12 database contains a schema with multiple related tables. Data was accidentally removed by executing TRUNCATE ... CASCADE . The schema and table definitions still exist, including their columns, data types, indexes, and relationships. However, the rows in the affected tables are gone, and queries such as SELECT COUNT(*) return zero. No usable backup from before the incident is available, and WAL archiving was disabled. However, the underlying disk may still contain remnants of old PostgreSQL heap pages or previous relation files. Questions: Is it possible to recover rows from raw disk pages after TRUNCATE CASCADE ? Can remaining WAL segments help reconstruct the deleted data if the required segments are still available? How can historical relation files or raw heap tuples be reliably associated with their original schema and tables? Which tools and recovery techniques are recommended for extracting surviving records without overwriting potentially recoverable data? What are the realistic recovery chances after TRUNCATE CASCADE , and which technical factors determine whether recovery is possible? I am looking for a safe, evidence-based recovery approach that does not rely on a backup and minimizes the risk of overwriting any remaining recoverable data.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: How to safely begin untangling async void usage in large codebase mostly in non-UI library code?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: In theory only permissible use of async void is for top level event handlers (and really only UI ones since "safety" also relies on a SyncronizationContext being present). Now, from my experience in practice people have used async void in code-bases in lots of other places, non-UI event-handlers mostly. Sometimes, due to not knowing better, sometimes due to being too clever coupling it with other signaling mechanisms (such as ManualResetEventSlim s). In a complex and large legacy system, it's relatively difficult to know where we silently rely on the async void being a fire forget that's not blocking something that we don't want blocked for too long a mile away in the call stack. So, the question is how to even begin untangling a messy codebase that needs to slowly migrate to something more sane. I thought of maybe creating a custom SynchronizationContext to at least log/get diagnostic data of when those operations start/finish, but that's going to present some challenges in changing multiple callsites that rely on Task.Run() and I might lose the context that I have set up at the program root.

The problem I've got is that the ThreadHint attribute is the last one in the tag so has the closing > which is invalid xml and can't be reopened in Visual Studio. My thinking is that I can solve this by doing a replace rather than a delete, so I can remove the whole line (as the delete does) and replace it with a > . That should result in valid xml but with the attribute removed. From what I've understood of the sed documentation I think I want to change the d to a g and provide the replacement value: [filter "stripthreadhint"] clean = sed '/ThreadHint=/>/g' smudge = cat That's not working, though, and results in the filter simply being skipped. Any suggestions on how I can do this? I'm not particularly wedded to the clean filter aproach so I'm open to any better suggestions.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Why does my Intl-based RFC 5545 date resolver select the wrong side of Samoa's 24-hour time-zone transition?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: Background and research context While investigating calendar boundary conditions in connection with Beta Calendars , a printable-calendar project I am affiliated with, I became interested in a distinction that is easy to overlook: a valid Gregorian calendar date is not necessarily a local date that actually occurred in every IANA time zone. That investigation led me to examine the interaction between RFC 5545 recurrence rules, local civil-time resolution, and historical IANA time-zone transitions. The particularly difficult case is Pacific/Apia , where an entire calendar date disappeared in December 2011. The project link provides background on the calendar work that motivated my investigation; the reproduction below is independent of the website. The recurrence scenario Consider the following iCalendar recurrence: DTSTART;TZID=Pacific/Apia:20110930T233000 RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;COUNT=6;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR;BYSETPOS=-1 The intended rule selects the last weekday of every month at 23:30 local time. For December 2011, the nominal last weekday is Friday, December 30. However, Samoa skipped December 30, 2011, during its transition across the International Date Line. The local clock advanced from December 29 directly to December 31. This creates an unusual situation: The Gregorian date is mathematically valid. The BYDAY rule matches Friday. BYSETPOS=-1 selects December 30. The selected local date-time does not exist in Pacific/Apia . RFC 5545 defines special interpretation rules for nonexistent local date-times.
